title: How to Get "Blood from a Turnip" by Highlighting Naysayers
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart describes a PD facilitation technique that transforms skeptical or resistant participant comments into instructional material rather than ignoring them. After a principal reported getting 'blood from a turnip' — something unexpected from somewhere it shouldn't have come — Stuart reconstructed the session practice that produced this result: reading all pre-session discussion comments, grouping them thematically, and then displaying even the most negative ones anonymously on screen, engaging with what was intelligent or valid in each. Stuart names this as an application of Gerald Graff's rhetorical 'name the naysayers' move, adapted for live PD. By affording resistant voices dignity and intellectual seriousness, he found that teachers who had been expressing cynicism became authentic participants. The article argues that negative commentary is not an obstacle to PD but valuable signal — and that the key facilitation move is dignifying the signal rather than suppressing it.
points: Resistant or negative comments in PD pre-work are not obstacles but useful signals; reading and organizing them before a session turns them into teachable material.

Displaying anonymous skeptical comments on screen during a live session, and engaging with what is intelligent or connected in them, is a concrete way to honor resistance and unlock authentic participation.
This technique borrows from Gerald Graff's 'name the naysayers' rhetorical strategy, which holds that acknowledging opposition publicly strengthens rather than weakens a facilitator's position.
Every human being in a PD room has inherent dignity regardless of what they are currently expressing; treating resistant participants as intellectually serious shifts the energy of the whole room.
Negative PD commentary that looks like a dead end often turns out to be an entry point — the exact 'blood from a turnip' moment that signals genuine engagement has begun.
quotes: The first thing I did was look up what it meant — I, like the principal, didn't know. I discovered that it meant getting something to come from something else that the first thing shouldn't be able to come from.

The next thing I did was think back on the experience the principal was referencing. It was early winter, and faculty was feeling the drag of that time of year. For this particular PD program, we were giving faculty a brief, video-based discussion prompt each month, hosted on their school's learning management platform.
In the discussion, there were lots of comments that, on their face, were pretty negative.

So prior to the hour-long live session with this group, all I did was read through their comments and group them on some slides (names removed) according to the day's topic (in this case, we were looking at the Effort and Efficacy beliefs). I pointed out promising practices, smart thoughts, and general connections between what folks had shared and how the Effort and Efficacy beliefs work.

But then once in a while, I would also point out some of these negative comments. (Again: names were removed.) They'd be right up there on the screen-share for all to see. And I'd point at specific things commenters said that I thought were interesting or intelligent or connected to how Effort and Efficacy work.

This is basically an old-school Gerald Graff move — name the naysayers. I did that, and I afforded them dignity. Because every human being we work with HAS dignity, regardless of the behaviors or thoughts they are currently sharing.
